titre: Federalist No. 10 (1787): Madison Sets Republic Against Democracy
accroche: Madison presents the representative republic as the remedy that direct democracy does not provide.
contenu_vulgarise:
In November 1787, as the American states debated ratification of the Constitution, James Madison published in the New York press, under the collective pseudonym “Publius,” the tenth in a series of essays favorable to the text, later gathered under the title *The Federalist*. It is cited today to defend “American democracy.” Yet Madison, in this text, uses the word in a precise sense and does not make it his model.

## Two Words Madison Distinguishes

He first defines a “pure democracy”: a society made up of a small number of citizens, who assemble and administer the government themselves. He contrasts it with the “republic,” which he defines as a government in which the system of representation operates. For him, the difference is not a quarrel over vocabulary: it concerns the way of dealing with what he calls factions, those groups of citizens united by a passion or an interest contrary to the rights of others or to the general interest.

## The Remedy of Extent

Madison's reasoning is that representation and, above all, the extent of the territory protect better against an oppressive majority. In a vast republic, interests are more varied, and it becomes harder to bring together a majority around a single unjust project. What many hold to be a handicap, the large size of a state, is therefore for him an advantage. The thesis runs against the idea, which the opponents of the Constitution (the Anti-Federalists) based on Montesquieu, that a republic must remain small: Madison and Montesquieu diverge on this question.

## What He Must Not Be Made to Say

This is not a text against the people: Madison's republic draws its power from the people, through the election of representatives. It is a text about how to organize popular sovereignty so that it does not turn against some of the citizens. To read it as praise of “democracy” in the current sense, or conversely as a rejection of voting, is to make it say something other than what it writes.

## Why It Still Matters

The distinction sheds light on a frequent confusion of vocabulary: the word “democracy” now designates representative regimes that Madison would have called republics. Reading his text with the 18th-century meaning avoids attributing to him a disagreement with our democracies, when he was discussing something else: the risk that a majority of citizens, united by a common interest, will crush the rights of a minority. It is this worry, more than the choice of a word, that structures the whole essay. It is also striking to note that the solution proposed is not greater power for an elite: it is the multiplication of interests within an enlarged framework.

repere.texte: Madison writes that a republic, a “government in which the system of representation operates,” “opens a different prospect, and promises the cure for which we are seeking” against factions.

carte.punch: Madison does not defend “democracy” there: he prefers the republic.
carte.idee: In Federalist No. 10 (1787), “pure democracy” means a small group that governs in assembly. Madison contrasts it with the representative republic and thinks that a vast territory protects better against unjust majorities.

quiz.question: What does Madison say about “democracy” in Federalist No. 10?
choix: He defends it as the best possible regime and rejects the representation of citizens
He judges it impossible to achieve in any society, even a small one
He equates it with a monarchy whose sovereign would be chosen by election
He defines it as a small group that governs in person, and prefers the republic
quiz.explication: Madison defines pure democracy as a society of few citizens who administer the government in person, and the republic by representation, which he judges better able to contain factions.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Under what name does Madison publish his essays, including Federalist No. 10, in 1787?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Madison publishes his essays in the New York press under the collective pseudonym Publius; Cato and Brutus are pseudonyms of Anti-Federalist opponents, and Cincinnatus does not appear in this story.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Madison, what best protects a republic against an oppressive majority?
choix: A restricted territory, as Montesquieu advocated
The extent of the territory, which multiplies and diversifies interests
A single leader endowed with extensive powers
Removing the right to vote from minority groups
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Madison maintains that a vast territory multiplies interests and makes it harder to form a majority united around an unjust project, contrary to the thesis of Montesquieu taken up by the Anti-Federalists.
